name: Karl Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a battery-cell winding line. My two-year technical diploma covered tension and seal testing; I can usually hear an uneven reel before the screen flags it. I like a tray of clean sealed cells, but clearing a rejected roll is slow and needs careful isolation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a public library. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about a year of expenses saved. My wage is higher than usual for this job, and plenty of similar plants are nearby. I use AI every day to group fault codes, then test the physical cells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cell crew AI is useful for grouping winding faults, but a battery still needs a safe seal. If the large promises fade, I will keep testing actual cells. Nobody should use an attractive chart as a fire barrier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the battery-cell winding line and earn above the usual operator rate. My partner works steady hours at a public library, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. We have about a year of expenses saved and plenty of similar plants nearby. Our current money is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting winding tension and testing the first sealed cell of each run. I use AI every day to group fault codes, and I check its clusters against physical test cells. I'll take the next offered paid safety refresher on the line because I want the younger operators to see how a failed seal is isolated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A reliable wage and a careful seal let me go home without worrying about a failed cell in someone's device.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which defect did the fault chart miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a cluster looked like a sensor fault, but the test cell had a small seal gap. We stopped winding and checked the heat jaw before another tray went through. A battery seal is judged by the cell, not the prettiest fault chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the reserve fit your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library wage is steady but smaller than mine. We pay the mortgage from both wages and built the reserve over many years. School costs still come out first each month. I would not risk the reserve on a machine idea I cannot test.

say: An **AI fault cluster** cannot certify a safe battery seal.
The crew needs **physical test cells** after each winding change.
think: My **higher line wage** and year-long reserve secure current bills.
The **library wage** and plentiful local plants offer further options.
do: **Keep** checking winding tension and first sealed cells after every reel change.
**Attend** offered paid safety refresher beside the cell line.
feel: **Calm** about current paid work and family finances.
S0.quote: A battery seal is judged by the cell, not the prettiest fault chart.
fieldNote: Karl **uses AI daily** to group faults and checks every conclusion against test cells.
His **strong reserve** and higher wage support calm, while a paid safety refresher keeps existing skills current.

steps.text: Keep setting battery winder and testing first sealed cells

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may plan cell orders and inspect test records before robots replace hands at a winding line. I would test a new camera on cells with known gaps before letting it sign anything. The crew should be paid to learn the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a new camera quickly, and the year saved gives us room. Still, management could run two winders with one lead and cut my higher-paid hours. The library wage alone would not cover the mortgage. Plenty of nearby plants does not mean the same base rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a written crew roster and paid guarded trial on the camera. If the plant offers a trainer-led place with test cells, I'll practise the reject and safe isolation controls. I'll also use a new AI image checker on anonymised seal photographs, then compare each flagged gap with a physical cell before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible lost high-rate shift, but I can test the change carefully. A camera that catches a gap is useful; a missing wage is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the camera trial stay safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a deliberately weak seal through the camera and ask the trainer to show how to stop the winder. A safe trial needs a locked line and a real reject. I would not learn this during an ordinary production rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about staffing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see base paid hours and who signs the safety release. If the roster combines two lines, I will ask the workers' group to challenge the change. A chart cannot tell us how many families lost a shift.

say: **AI planning** may change cell orders before robots wind batteries.
A **camera test** needs known weak seals and paid instruction.
think: A combined **winder roster** could cut my high-rate hours.
The **library wage** and long reserve do not guarantee equal replacement pay.
do: **Request** paid guarded camera trial and written crew roster.
**Learn** camera rejects on test cells if trainer place offered.
**Try** new AI image checks and verify flagged seals on physical cells.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic cut to higher-paid hours.
S1.quote: A chart cannot tell us how many families lost a shift.
fieldNote: His **new AI skill** checks seal images, beyond his usual fault-code grouping.
He wants a **paid guarded camera place** and written staffing terms before accepting combined lines.

steps.text: Request written battery crew roster before accepting new target

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cell crew thinking AI could plan production by 2028, then capable robots around 2031 could wind and inspect every battery cell. I would ask for a written staffing plan and paid safety roles. I want my team to know the date before a shift is removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots can do the physical winding. My higher-paid lead shift could be cut, and the library wage would not cover our mortgage alone. A year saved and many nearby plants allow time to look, though I cannot assume any will pay my current rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the manager for a written robot timetable and the base pay of any safety posts. If the plant offers funded paid-time training in battery safety inspection with guarded hands-on work, I'll enrol. If my hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local cell-production jobs only if regular pay, travel and school hours fit; after qualifying, I'll also apply to posted local inspection roles under those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the high rate, but not stranded. I can compare a real offer while the reserve covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should battery-safety training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practical test should make me isolate the winding line, spot a weak seal and reject a cell before it heats. A trainer should sign each step. A certificate without a guarded stop would be worthless beside a live battery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes another cell plant viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fallback production job needs a real local posting and a base rate after travel that covers our mortgage. I would check its shift against the children's school hours and my partner's library hours. If the net pay falls short, I keep searching.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes production plans before robots wind cells around 2031.
A **written crew date** and paid safety roles matter now.
think: At **48**, I could lose the higher-paid lead shift.

do: **Ask** manager for robot schedule and paid safety posts.
**Enrol** in funded paid guarded battery inspection if offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local production or qualified inspection if cut and net pay fits.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible high-rate loss with resources to act.
S2.quote: A certificate without a guarded stop would be worthless beside a live battery.
fieldNote: His **higher-wage risk** is realistic, but a year of savings and many plants allow a controlled search.
The **production fallback** and qualified inspection application require safe local posts and net pay and school-compatible shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan cell orders in 2031 and capable robots wind them around 2034. Five years lets a plant pay for practical safety teaching before any crew shrinks. I'd want posted jobs beside the course notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots can do the line work. The children will be older, but the mortgage may still need my higher wage. My diploma helps with the measurements; a safety certificate might add a second option, if real local employers still hire inspectors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll put new money from each full higher-rate payday into our reserve after bills. I'll ask for a recognized cell-inspection certificate with covered fees, paid release and guarded line practice. If an actual seat is offered, I'll enrol; once qualified, if winder hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local inspection work only where net base pay and school travel fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the later rate, though I can check paid training while I still earn. A qualification only helps when somebody offers a wage for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical assessment involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a weak seal, isolate the winder and run a test cell with a trainer watching. The written assessment should include what to do with a rejected tray. I would not use the family reserve for unpaid practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare inspection pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted inspection job must state base wages, worksite and travel days. A distant plant with a better hourly rate can leave less after fuel and child pickup. I would calculate the net before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan cell orders in 2036 and capable robots could wind them around 2039. A decade lets the factory train people before changing the line. I would ask the workers' group to get paid practice written into any plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when robots do the hands-on winding. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage is paid. A year saved and many nearby plants give options if the high-rate shifts and real vacancies last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the winder and pay extra mortgage principal from newly earned full wages after bills. I'll attend the workers' group meeting each quarter to ask for offered paid inspection seats and actual posts. If a funded paid guarded place with a trainer is offered, I'll take it; after qualifying, if my line hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local safety jobs only if net base pay and travel work for our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant change, while current wages are secure. I can ask for a written role before giving up one I hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the worker plan need to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agreement should say who keeps paid stop authority, who trains inspectors and how many jobs are posted. I would have a technician and an operator check the terms together. A safety plan without a paid person on the line is paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a safety role workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting needs its base rate, travel days and shift times. My partner's library hours help with pickup but not every evening. A role with unpaid travel and a lower net wage would not be sensible, even with a stronger title.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut the higher-paid winding role before I have another one. A written staffing date, an offered funded paid safety seat and posted safe local work with enough net pay would help. I would compare the school hours too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the first battery cell after a robot resets the winder. A failed seal can wait quietly until the battery warms in someone's hand.

headlineQuote: A failed seal can wait quietly until the battery warms in someone's hand.
portrait: **Karl**, 43, is a skilled senior battery-cell lead with a two-year technical diploma, higher pay and a year saved.
He and his library-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with many similar plants nearby.
His **progressive outlook** leads to workers-group action, while daily AI use prompts careful new image tests.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about losing the high wage; offered safety training and net local pay guide his response.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable cell-winding robots around 2031 and cut his higher-paid shift.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing date**, funded paid safety training and posted safe local work at sufficient net pay would help.
